summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Internet Area standards-track and experimental documents. The goal is to identify dependencies so protocols can be redesigned to be address independent or support both IPv4 and IPv6. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of rules in one area that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in internet area specs
what ipv4 dependencies exist in internet protocols
how does dhcp work with ipv6
subtitle: Detailed survey of IPv4 dependencies in Internet Area protocols like DNS, DHCP, and IPv6 transition mechanisms.

tldr.problem: The Internet Area of IETF standards includes critical protocols like DNS and DHCP that enable addressing, discovery, and configuration across the network. Many were designed assuming IPv4 would be primary.
tldr.mechanism: This survey examines 186 Internet Area RFCs (Full, Draft, Proposed Standards, and Experimental) to identify which ones have IPv4 dependencies and how severe those dependencies are. It documents protocols like BOOTP, DHCP, DNS, and PPP variants.
tldr.outcome: The Internet Area was found to have 52 RFCs with IPv4 dependencies (28%), including many of the most widely deployed protocols. However, many were already being extended or redesigned to support IPv6 simultaneously.

today: RFC 3790 remains informational. It served as a detailed reference for protocol designers working on IPv6 transition mechanisms in the Internet Area. Many of the identified dependencies have since been addressed through dual-stack implementations, tunneling mechanisms, and parallel IPv6 versions of key protocols like DNS and DHCP.

sections.title: The Internet Area and Its Role
sections.content:
The Internet Area of the IETF encompasses the core protocols that allow the Internet to function: IP itself, DNS for name resolution, DHCP for address configuration, ARP for address resolution, and many protocols for transmission over specific physical media. These 186 RFCs form the backbone of Internet operations. Unlike routing-specific protocols or application-layer protocols, changes to the Internet Area affect every device on the network.

This makes the Internet Area both critical and challenging for IPv6 transition. Protocols like DNS must continue to work during the transition and must be able to handle both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Configuration protocols like DHCP must be able to provide either type of address depending on client capability.
sections.plainLanguage: This area covers the most fundamental rules of how computers talk to each other: finding the computer you want, getting an address, and sending data. Because everyone uses these rules, updating them is very important.

sections.title: Full Standards with IPv4 Dependencies
sections.content:
Among the 24 Full Standards in the Internet Area, 17 (70.8%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include foundational protocols: RFC 791 (IPv4 itself), RFC 792 (ICMP), RFC 826 (ARP), RFC 894 (IP over Ethernet), RFC 903 (Reverse ARP), RFC 919 and RFC 922 (broadcast mechanisms), RFC 950 (subnetting), RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 (DNS), RFC 1042 (IP over IEEE 802), and others.

Many of these are essential network fundamentals. RFC 1122 (Requirements for Internet Hosts) is referenced across many other standards but contains IPv4-specific requirements. The DNS standards (RFC 1034 and 1035) are critical for name resolution but were written before IPv6 existed. All of these needed to be examined for how they could be extended or redesigned to support IPv6 without breaking existing IPv4 functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Nearly all the oldest and most important rules mention old addresses. This includes the rules about how to find a computer by name, how to ask for an address, and how to send information over different types of wires.

sections.title: Draft and Proposed Standards
sections.content:
Among the 20 Draft Standards in the Internet Area, only 6 (30%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include RFC 951 (BOOTP), RFC 2131 (DHCP), RFC 2132 (DHCP Options), RFC 2390 (Inverse ARP), and several PPP-related RFCs. Notably, RFC 2460 (IPv6 Specification), RFC 2461 (IPv6 Neighbor Discovery), RFC 2462 (IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration), and RFC 2463 (ICMPv6) are IPv6-focused and do not require discussion in this context.

Among the 111 Proposed Standards, 22 (19.9%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include tunneling mechanisms, Mobile IP, various PPP control protocols, DNS extensions, and DHCP options. The lower percentage here reflects that newer protocol proposals are increasingly designed with IPv6 in mind or are more flexible about address formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer rules are much less likely to only work with old addresses. About one-third of the middle-level rules mention old addresses, and only about one-fifth of the newest proposed rules do.

sections.title: IPv6 Transition and Dual-Stack Protocols
sections.content:
Several key protocols support or enable IPv6 transition. DHCP Options (RFC 2132) and related RFCs define options that allow IPv4 clients to receive configuration information. Parallel standards exist for IPv6: Neighbor Discovery (RFC 2461), Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 2462), and ICMPv6 (RFC 2463) provide equivalent functionality for IPv6 networks.

Tunneling mechanisms like IP Encapsulation within IP (RFC 2003), Generic Routing Encapsulation (RFC 2784), L2TP (RFC 2661), and 6to4 mechanisms enable IPv6 to run inside IPv4 networks during transition. Many PPP-related protocols (RFC 2472 is IPv6 over PPP) allow point-to-point links to carry both protocol versions. The survey shows that while the Internet Area has heavy IPv4 dependencies, the transition infrastructure is already being built in parallel.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of new rules let computers talk to each other in either old or new address styles at the same time. There are also tricks to send new-style addresses through old-style networks while the whole Internet is changing over.

sections.title: Experimental Approaches and Alternatives
sections.content:
The Internet Area includes 31 Experimental RFCs, of which 7 (22.6%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include experimental DNS mechanisms (RFC 1183, RFC 2009), experimental tunneling and encapsulation schemes (RFC 1226, RFC 1241), IPv6 testing address allocation (RFC 2471), and various alternative routing and addressing proposals.

Experimental RFCs provide a space to explore alternative approaches that might not be standardized. Some, like the 6to4 anycast prefix mechanisms, eventually become widely deployed despite their experimental status. Others represent dead-end proposals that were superseded by the main standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: The experimental rules are things people are trying out but are not sure about yet. Some of them work with old addresses, some work with new ones, and some try to make both work together.
